props.title: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari
props.initialSlug: Madman manipulates sleepwalker to commit murder

sections.content: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari revolutionized cinema with its expressionist nightmare vision. Director Robert Wiene twisted reality through painted shadows, tilted sets, and geometric distortions that externalized psychological trauma. The film's influence echoes through horror and noir, from Nosferatu (1922) to Metropolis (1927) to modern psychological thrillers like Shutter Island (2010). Its unreliable narrator twist ending predated Fight Club (1999) by nearly 80 years, while its asylum-frame story inspired everything from One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest (1975) to Sucker Punch (2011).

sections.content: The film's visual style created a template for cinematic horror. The jagged architecture and harsh angles influenced Universal horror classics like Dracula (1931) and Frankenstein (1931). German Expressionism's emphasis on psychological states through visual design carried forward to film noir, seen in Double Indemnity (1944) and The Third Man (1949). Modern directors like Tim Burton explicitly reference Caligari's style - Edward Scissorhands (1990) and The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993) are direct descendants.

Caligari's exploration of authority, madness, and reality's fragility resonates with contemporary films. Black Swan (2010) uses similar techniques to portray psychological breakdown, while Inception (2010) plays with dream architecture that recalls Caligari's twisted sets. The film's influence on horror extends to The Babadook (2014) and A Cure for Wellness (2016), which both draw on its asylum imagery and questioning of reality. SUBHEAD: Legacy in Modern Cinema

The film's innovative narrative structure continues to inspire. Shutter Island (2010) directly references Caligari's asylum-twist ending, while The Sixth Sense (1999) employs similar unreliable narrator techniques. The blurring of reality and madness influences psychological horror like Jacob's Ladder (1990) and Session 9 (2001). Even found-footage horror owes a debt to Caligari's frame narrative structure.
